title: What is Learning? - 1
author: Martin Skelton
summary: This fourth post begins building a usable, evidence-based definition of learning by asking where most learning in schools takes place. Skelton's answer is the learners' brains, which makes classrooms, homework, trips, teaching and parenting factors that affect learning rather than learning itself. He explains neurons in plain terms, with the cell body, dendrites, axon and synapse mapped onto a hand and arm, stressing that their basic behaviour is evolutionarily hard-wired. From this he derives an embryonic idea that learning occurs when a neuronal chain is created, lengthened or joined into a more complex network. He suggests a teacher's key job is to provide experiences that make those chains form, and he reinterprets his early teaching failure as students being busy but not chaining. He cautions that brain research is full of hypotheses and that some claims do not hold up in real classrooms.
points: Most learning takes place in the learner's brain, so everything in the school is a factor that affects learning rather than learning itself.
Neurons behave in a largely hard-wired way, chaining from one to the next whenever a stimulus triggers them.
A provisional definition emerges: learning happens when a neuronal chain is created, made larger, or joined into a more complex network.
A teacher's role is to provide opportunities for students' brains to create, lengthen and link chains.
Skelton warns that some brain-research claims are unproven and have been over-applied to classrooms and homes.
quotes: The actual answer to where most learning takes place in schools - and here’s the part that you might think was just a trick - is: In the learners’ brains.

First, because it places learning in the right place and establishes classrooms, school buildings, homework, school journeys, teaching and parenting and much more for what they are: factors that affect learning.
Unfortunately, this hasn't prevented some writers making claims for those discoveries that simply can't be stood up with humans or in the real-life messiness of classrooms and homes.

Because neurons are evolutionarily hard-wired, the second neuron behaves just like the first and the third just like the second. All other things being equal, this process is designed to happen automatically.

We might, at this point, have a very embryonic, brain-based idea of learning beginning to come into focus. It is anything but complete but, without being remotely definitive (yet), we can begin to see that learning begins to happen in the brain when either a new neuronal chain is created, made larger or an existing neuronal chain becomes part of a more complex network.

Nothing I was asking them to do was challenging enough to cause their neurons to do what they were hard-wired to do. My students weren’t creating new neuronal chains, they weren’t extending existing neuronal chains and they weren’t linking existing chains to each other.
